name: Grace Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll be honest, I don't usually do things like this, but my union rep said these panels are worth talking to. Just don't expect me to know much about computers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a night response team out of the Harbour Road station on the east side, so I start at ten at night and finish at seven. It's calls back to back: domestics, drunk fights outside the kebab shops, a shoplifter the security guard is sitting on. I'm still in my second year, so my tutor constable Dev rides with me a lot, and he still fixes half my reports. The part I love is the people, even the rough ones. The part that wears me out is the paperwork at four in the morning when my eyes won't stay open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like what I already think is going on. Lots of noise, a few gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly. At the station there's always some new system that's going to change everything, and a year later we're back to doing it the old way with a few extra clicks. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should have gone on more officers instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays my job, which I'm glad about. I'm not good with the tech, and I was dreading being pushed into some app I don't understand. I'd still have the same problems, though: short-staffed nights, too many calls, and me slow on the reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep working on my reports with Dev until I can write them alone. I'd put the same 500 a month into savings that I do now. And I'd keep going to the union branch meetings, because staffing is the fight, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. I've got a good cushion, about nine months of pay put by, and Sam's job at the hospital isn't going anywhere. So I'd sleep fine, or as fine as you sleep on nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the old way with a few extra clicks. Is there a system like that now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a body camera tool that writes up what was said into a draft statement, and it got a woman's name wrong. I tried the body camera tool twice and it called a knife a 'nice'. I switched it off and nobody's made me turn it back on, so I just type.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a quiet sign that things really are fine look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the sergeant stops sending emails about the new tool of the month. When the rota has five of us on a Friday night instead of three. That's what fine looks like at Harbour Road.

say: I'd say the hype was **just hype**, like most new systems the station gets.
I'd argue online the money should have gone on **more officers** instead of gadgets.
think: I'm quietly **relieved**, because I'm slow with technology and was dreading new apps.
My real problems stay the same: **short-staffed nights**, too many calls and slow reports.
do: Keep practising reports with **my tutor** Dev until I can write them alone.
Keep saving **500 a month** on top of about nine months of pay already saved.
Keep attending **union branch** meetings to push for better night staffing.
feel: She feels **relieved** and secure, with savings and a partner in a steady hospital job.
S0.quote: I tried the body camera tool twice and it called a knife a 'nice'. I switched it off and nobody's made me turn it back on, so I just type.
fieldNote: She frames everything through **staffing**, not technology; robots barely register as the real problem.
She switched off the **body camera** drafting tool after it garbled a statement, and nobody pushed back.
Her calm is earned by **savings** and her partner's job, not by confidence in her own skills.

steps.text: Keep practising written reports with Dev until she can write them alone
Keep putting 500 a month into savings
Attend every union branch meeting about night-shift staffing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels more real. The reports and the call handling are exactly the kind of thing they'd hand to a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table before any of it gets switched on. With my friends I'd say it's the bosses saving money again, dressed up as progress. I'd sign every petition going about keeping humans on the phones in the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of what I'm bad at would get done by software, and that's a strange thing to admit. If the report writes itself, then the thing that makes me a weak officer kind of disappears. But I'd also worry they'd use it to run nights with even fewer of us, because the computer handles the paperwork so why do you need the fifth officer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the union's working group on new technology, even though I know nothing about the technology, because someone needs to speak for the night shifts. I'd ask Dev to show me the new tools slowly, one at a time, rather than getting thrown in. And I'd keep my savings where they are, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's still there, I'm sure of that, but everything around it would be shifting under my feet. I don't like learning new screens; it makes me feel stupid in front of the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The call handlers in the control room, definitely. My friend Priya works there, and her whole job is answering and logging calls. If a computer answers the 999 line, she's out, and she's got a little boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the software would fix what you're weakest at, but you'd also fight it. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I'd take the help with the typing, but I'd fight them using it as an excuse to cut people. Those are two different things, and the union knows the difference even if management pretends not to.

say: I'd demand the **union** gets a seat before any new system goes live.
I'd call it **bosses saving money** and sign petitions to keep humans answering emergency calls.
think: Software could fix my **weakest skill**, writing reports, which is strange to admit.
I fear management would use it to run nights with **fewer officers**.
do: Join the union's **technology working group** to speak up for night shifts.
Ask Dev to teach the new tools **one at a time** rather than all at once.
Leave her **savings** untouched as a buffer.
feel: She feels **uneasy**: her job is safe but she dreads looking slow on new screens.
S1.quote: If the report writes itself, then the thing that makes me a weak officer kind of disappears.
fieldNote: She openly admits software would cover her **weakness**, yet resists it on principle about staffing.
Her real worry is for **control-room** friends like Priya, not herself.
She separates **help with typing** from cuts, a distinction she trusts the union to defend.

steps.text: Join the union working group on new technology at the force
Learn each new reporting tool one at a time with Dev
Keep the nine months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not much. I'd only just be off probation properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that policing needs people, because you can't hand a crying kid to a computer. Online I'd be angry, pushing for laws that say only a sworn human officer can arrest someone. I'd be at every union rally they called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the desk side of policing would be gone by 2028: the reports, the case files, the planning of who goes where. That's maybe a third of my shift. Then by 2031 the robots come for the walking and driving and holding someone down, and I'm a junior who's not great at the job, so I'd be near the front of the queue to go. My savings would carry me a while, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union straight away and push for a no-redundancy deal for sworn officers. I'd write to my city councillor about a law that keeps arrests in human hands. And I'd stop spending on the holiday Sam and I were planning, and put that 3,000 into savings instead. I don't think I'd retrain; I wouldn't know into what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest, and angry underneath it. I picture standing at the Harbour Road front desk while a machine does the thing I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd still be out on the street doing the hands-on part, the doors and the fights, while all the thinking gets taken off me. So for three years I'd be a body in a uniform taking orders from a screen. I'm not sure that's a job I'd want, but it would pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sam I might need to lean on the hospital wage for a while, and I'd hate saying it. Sam would just say we'll be fine, because that's what Sam always says. Then I'd lie awake doing the maths on the savings.

say: I'd insist **policing needs people**, because nobody can hand a crying child to a computer.
I'd campaign for laws saying only a **sworn human officer** can make an arrest.
think: The **desk third** of my shift, reports and case files, would be gone by 2028.
Once **robots arrive in 2031**, a weak junior like me would be first to go.
do: Press the union for a **no-redundancy deal** covering sworn officers.
Write to her **city councillor** about keeping arrests in human hands.
Cancel the planned holiday and **save the 3,000** instead.
feel: She feels **scared** and angry, picturing herself sidelined at the station front desk.
S2.quote: For three years I'd be a body in a uniform taking orders from a screen. I'm not sure that's a job I'd want, but it would pay the rent.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** before robots feels to her like a hollowed-out job, not a reprieve.
She has **no retraining idea** at all, which is where her resistance to change bites.
Her savings and her partner's wage turn panic into **anxiety**, but she still does the maths at night.

steps.text: Press the union for a no-redundancy deal for sworn officers
Write to her city councillor asking for human-only arrests by law
Cancel the planned holiday and save the 3,000 instead
Lean on Sam's hospital wage if her pay drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two. Not much better, but I'd at least be properly trained by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things as with the fast one: keep humans in policing, protect the officers who keep people safe. But with five years I'd say we have time to get the rules written properly, so there's no excuse for the government not to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gets me to 32, with a bit of experience, which helps. But I'm still not someone who's good at new things, so I'd be watching the people who are pick up the new roles while I stay where I am. Robots in 2034 would still catch me in the middle of my career, and I'd still be the one who never learned the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand for the union branch committee, because with five years there's time to get a real agreement on paper. I'd push for training that starts slow for people like me. And I'd keep saving, maybe up to a year's pay, before 2031. I'd probably also take the sergeant's exam prep course the force offers, even though the thought makes me queasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but in a slower, grinding way rather than a panic. Five years feels like knowing a test is coming and you never studied for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the sergeant's course makes you queasy. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's all about planning and managing, and that's exactly the thinking work that goes first. I'd be studying for the part of the job that disappears. But a sergeant still leads people on the street, so maybe it buys me the hands-on years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or plan would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I wanted to buy a flat near the hospital in about three years. I think I'd hold off until I knew where I stood with the force. Renting is annoying, but at least you can leave.

say: I'd repeat that **policing needs humans** and push for officer protections.
I'd say five years leaves **no excuse** for the government not to write proper rules.
think: Five years brings **experience**, but I'd still watch quicker colleagues grab the new roles.
Robots in **2034** would still hit me in the middle of my career.
do: Stand for the **union branch committee** to secure a written agreement.
Push the force for **slow-start training** for officers who struggle with technology.
Build savings toward **a year's pay** before 2031.
feel: She feels a slow, **grinding worry**, like facing a test she never studied for.
S3.quote: Five years feels like knowing a test is coming and you never studied for it.
fieldNote: She'd study for **sergeant** while knowing planning work goes first, an honest contradiction.
The **flat purchase** with her partner is the first plan she would freeze.
More time shifts her from protest to **negotiation**, but not toward retraining herself.

steps.text: Stand for the union branch committee to negotiate a written agreement
Take the force's sergeant exam preparation course
Save toward a full year's pay before 2031
Delay buying the flat near the hospital with Sam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. That's a whole different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when governments have no excuse at all. Ten years is long enough to plan a fair way through, with retraining paid for and nobody thrown out. I'd say it at union meetings and I'd say it at the ballot box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years takes me to 37, and the robots come at 40. By then I'd have a proper career behind me and maybe a pension started. I'd still hate the change, but I'd have time to get used to it slowly, which is the only way I ever get used to anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going in the job and stop fretting. I'd vote for whoever promises a proper transition plan for public workers. I'd keep the union work going. Somewhere around year five I might look at the force's victim support or custody roles, because those are about people in a bad moment, and I'm good at that part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could live with it. It's like seeing weather coming from a long way off; you've got time to find your coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently between year one and year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, nothing much, just keep learning the job properly. Around year five, once I can see which jobs the machines are actually doing, I'd move toward the people-heavy roles. I don't want to jump early and land on the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first if you changed roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, before Sam even. My mum cleaned offices for thirty years and the union got her a pension. My mum would tell me to get it in writing, and she'd be right.

say: I'd say ten years leaves governments **no excuse** for leaving workers behind.
I'd push for **paid retraining** at union meetings and at the ballot box.
think: I'd be **37** at AGI and 40 when robots come, with a real career behind me.
Slow change is the **only way** I ever get used to anything new.
do: Keep working the job and **stop fretting** in the early years.
Vote for parties promising a **transition plan** for public workers.
Look at **victim support** or custody roles around year five.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but able to live with it, like weather seen far off.
S4.quote: My mum cleaned offices for thirty years and the union got her a pension. My mum would tell me to get it in writing, and she'd be right.
fieldNote: Her mother's **union pension** story shapes her instinct to get every promise in writing.
She wants to **wait and watch** before moving, fearing jumping early into the wrong role.
Ten years turns her **resistance** into something she can manage at her own slow pace.

steps.text: Keep working response nights and learning the job properly
Vote for a transition plan for public workers
Look at victim support or custody roles around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is a union deal in writing that protects sworn officers, and training that goes at the pace of people like me instead of the quick ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the control room. Everyone talks about officers on the street. The people answering the phones in the control room would go first, and they're mostly women on lower pay. Someone should be asking them.

headlineQuote: The people answering the phones in the control room would go first, and they're mostly women on lower pay. Someone should be asking them.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old** night response officer in her second year, still leaning on her tutor for reports.
She is **union-minded** and frames every change as a fight about staffing and fair treatment.
She avoids **technology** and switched off an AI drafting tool after it garbled a statement.
Her **savings** and partner's hospital job keep her calm in the slow worlds but anxious in fast ones.
With **ten years** she would drift toward people-heavy roles; with two she has no plan beyond protest.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because a weak junior like her would be near the front of the queue to go.
whatWouldHelp: A written **union deal** protecting sworn officers.
Training that moves at the **pace** of slower learners.
